title: Put Each Case in Its Setting
definition: The order in which events happened.
content:
Regional uprisings occurred in different places and periods. A comparison should begin with the case name, location and date before describing causes or actions. This mission studies three selected examples: Tamblot in Bohol in 1621, Sumuroy in Palapag, Samar, beginning in 1649, and the Basi Revolt in Ilocos in 1807. These are not all early uprisings, and their dates do not make them one coordinated event.

Our timeline puts the named cases in order. It is a modern teaching guide, not a map of every participant or a complete chronology of each case. Earlier does not mean less important, and a later event was not automatically caused by the earlier one. To establish a connection between cases, look for evidence of communication, influence or shared action. Similar opposition to colonial demands alone does not prove the same program, leadership or private motives.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: Keep a named uprising attached to its place and period.
Chronological order alone does not prove coordination or causation.
task: Three cases appear in date order. What does that establish most directly?
Their sequence, not proof that they were one coordinated event
One shared command for all cases
That each earlier case caused every later one
Every participants identical motive
reason: Their sequence, not proof that they were one coordinated event. Chronological order alone does not prove coordination or causation.

title: Tamblot: A Named Bohol Case
definition: A spiritual leader in the community setting discussed in this case.
content:
NCCA CulturEd identifies Tamblot as a babaylan who led an uprising in Bohol in 1621. Its account connects his movement with a wish to return to earlier religious practices. This introduces a particular religious concern within colonial change. It does not establish the thoughts or beliefs of every person in Bohol.

The entry also notes that much of Tamblots life is poorly documented. Do not fill those gaps with invented speeches, supernatural claims presented as verified events, or a complete biography. We study religious history without ranking faiths or requiring a student to adopt one. The uprising involved conflict and harm; no activity asks learners to perform a ritual or reenact an attack. Our source card keeps the named role, place, beginning and source limit visible. A leader and a concern are starting evidence, not every participants full motive or a universal explanation of all revolts.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: CulturEd names Tamblot, a babaylan, in Bohol.
The entry dates the uprising to 1621 and connects it with earlier religious practices.
Limited biographical records do not justify invented conversations or universal motives.
task: What does the Tamblot case support in this comparison?
A named Bohol uprising connected with a religious concern in 1621
Every Bohol resident had identical beliefs
All uprisings had the same cause
The source records every conversation
reason: A named Bohol uprising connected with a religious concern in 1621. Limited biographical records do not justify invented conversations or universal motives.

title: Sumuroy: Forced Labor and Abuses
definition: A concern or complaint about required work or working conditions.
content:
The NHCP marker identifies Agustin Sumuroy with Palapag, Samar, and an uprising beginning on 1 June 1649 against forced labor and abuses. The marker also describes the uprising spreading beyond its initial setting. This connects a labor grievance with a named action and period; it does not describe every local experience in places later affected.

Compare the initial case with any claim about wider participation. Spreading to another place is not proof that every resident joined, that every participant had one motive, or that every local action was identical. A later commemorative marker can preserve important information without being a transcript of every event. Our labelled source card is not an authentic participant list. Ask what particular action is recorded and what further evidence would help explain conditions, roles and outcomes. We acknowledge harm without graphic detail or points for fighting.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: The marker links Palapag and 1 June 1649 with Sumuroys uprising.
Forced labor and abuses are named concerns.
A wider affected area does not prove universal participation or identical local experience.
task: A marker describes spread beyond Palapag. What should not be assumed?
That every resident in each affected place joined with an identical motive
That Palapag is a named starting setting
That the source identifies labor concerns
That further local evidence could help
reason: That every resident in each affected place joined with an identical motive. A wider affected area does not prove universal participation or identical local experience.

title: Basi: Monopoly and Local Livelihoods
definition: Exclusive control of a particular trade or activity.
content:
The CCP account connects the Basi Revolt in Ilocos in 1807 with a government monopoly over basi, a sugarcane wine. The historical question concerns control of production and sale and its connection with opposition. This is a different setting and concern from the selected Bohol and Samar cases. It is not an invitation to use or make alcohol.

The account describes the later painting series by Esteban Villanueva, made in 1821, representing the 1807 revolt. Keep the event and the making of its depiction separate. The paintings were not cameras recording every word or motive. Our comparison uses a dated source guide rather than graphic images, drinking activities or a complete battle chronology. A monopoly connection does not explain every participants reasons or every households resources. Later lessons will explore outcomes and significance more closely, using evidence rather than assigning identical results to all early resistance.

clues: The Basi example concerns Ilocos in 1807 and opposition to a monopoly.
The event of 1807 and the painting series of 1821 are different stages.
A policy concern and later depiction do not reveal every participants motives.
task: A caption calls the 1821 paintings images made during the 1807 uprising. What correction fits?
Separate the event date from the later making of its depiction
Use 1807 as every images making date
Treat the paintings as cameras
Infer every exact speech from the images
reason: Separate the event date from the later making of its depiction. A policy concern and later depiction do not reveal every participants motives.

title: Compare Similarities Without Erasing Differences
definition: Examining similarities and differences using evidence from particular settings.
content:
The selected cases share opposition within Spanish colonial rule, but that similarity does not make their causes, people and actions identical. Tamblot, Sumuroy and Basi belong to distinct places and periods. Compare the same questions: where and when, which concern, what recorded action, whose participation and what evidence remains limited.

Our fictional comparison desk separates a CulturEd entry, a commemorative marker and an art-history account. These sources have different purposes and dates. A later account is not automatically an eyewitness record, and one leader is not a full participant list. Do not label every early uprising as already sharing one modern national program without evidence. Similar grievances can coexist with different local aims. If the source leaves an outcome or motive uncertain, name the limit instead of inventing unity, success or failure. The comparison cards are teaching aids, not original documents.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: Ask the same clear questions of each named case.
Similar opposition does not establish identical aims, people or coordination.
Entries, markers and art accounts support different claims and have their own limits.
task: Three cases opposed colonial demands. What is the strongest comparison?
Compare their distinct settings, concerns and recorded actions without assuming one program
Treat all as the same event
Assign every participant one modern national aim
Ignore source dates and purposes
reason: Compare their distinct settings, concerns and recorded actions without assuming one program. Entries, markers and art accounts support different claims and have their own limits.

title: Prepare Your Regional Comparison Report
definition: Examining similarities and differences using evidence from particular settings.
content: Review five ideas. Chronology puts cases in order without proving coordination. Tamblots 1621 Bohol case includes a religious concern and limited biographical evidence. Sumuroys Palapag case begins in 1649 and names forced labor and abuses. The 1807 Basi case connects with monopoly; the 1821 paintings are later depictions. Similar opposition does not establish identical causes or one shared command. Prepare a fictional comparison report for another Grade 5 learner. Name each case, place and period, compare a documented concern and recorded action, and identify a source limit. Do not assume every resident joined, use religion as every persons motive, or invent speeches and meetings. Keep harm visible without reenacting it or gaining points for it. The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. Review linked learning content before practice and a retry if needed. Completing this mission earns its configured reward once, but does not complete Chapter 12. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: Ask the same clear questions of each named case.
Similar opposition does not establish identical aims, people or coordination.
Entries, markers and art accounts support different claims and have their own limits.
task: Which report best compares early regional uprisings?
Keep cases and sources distinct while comparing documented concerns and actions
Treat every uprising as one coordinated event
Use one leader as every residents full story
Date every later depiction to its event
reason: Compare named regional cases through place, period, concerns, recorded actions and source limits without assuming identical participation or aims.
